entries.title: v0.0.2 to v0.0.4: the boundary tax
entries.summary: The host boundary stops walking the whole heap per re-entry; an O(heap) walk is removed from the interpreter-only WASM build; JSON.stringify ×4000 drops from 919 ms to 8.5 ms; wasm-opt is dropped after measurement.

blocks.text: The day after the first release, the first embedders' workloads exposed the cost of crossing into the VM. v0.0.2 (`a70cef47`) stopped the host boundary from walking the whole heap on every re-entry and raised parser sandbox limits that had rejected real code. v0.0.3 (`d71168a9`) removed another O(heap) walk, took `JSON.stringify` ×4000 from 919 ms to 8.5 ms, shrank the bundle from 6,018,862 to 5,668,533 raw bytes, dropped `wasm-opt` because `-Oz` measured smaller raw but larger on the wire and slower, and pre-warmed the playground Worker after finding that a 68 ms delay was V8 compiling, not the engine. v0.0.4 (`769c68ce`) added `getGlobalsFingerprint`, a content digest so a mutation through a reference cannot be missed, cutting per-tick host sync from 9.6 ms to 2.1 ms.

entries.title: v0.0.1: first distribution, README redesign, ledger archived
entries.summary: The first native and WebAssembly release; B249 takes bytecode-vm from 3.68× to 0.93× Node; module cycle roots restore 95,939 of 95,942; the performance ledger is archived at 881 KB.

blocks.text: `96dac4e1` is tagged v0.0.1. `be2f5ed4` (B249) records the retained-ten suite at 0.918× Node and hostile at 0.866×, with `bytecode-vm` from 3.68× to 0.93× and `warm-router` from 2.18× to 1.62×. `8ac5cc73` computes module `[[CycleRoot]]` at depth-first-search time and restores three Test262 rows, back to 95,939 of 95,942. `ce488bbe` archives the campaign ledger (B001 to B252, mostly negative results, with a header warning that its earliest sections were written at 3.31× and have since been refuted), and `ac183cff` redesigns the README around measurements.

entries.title: A 2.16× regression, root-caused and reversed in a day
entries.summary: A de-fused CallMethod lowering spikes the headline to 2.157× Node and drifts 24 Test262 rows; both are traced to one commit and reversed.

blocks.text: The capture on 29 August came in at 2.157× Node on the headline ten, from 0.965× the day before. The cause was `85fca98a`, which de-fused the `CallMethod` lowering; `e2250fca` separately traced a 24-row Test262 drift to the same change. `271647ad` reversed it (0.977× headline, 0.665× all 13). The same call-order question came back in September as B280, this time resolved in favour of correctness and with the cost measured.

entries.title: The hostile corpus goes under parity
entries.summary: The 17-row hostile suite, built to make JavaScript stop looking like an ideal reducer, records a geomean of 0.961× Node for the first time.

blocks.text: The hostile corpus pairs six baselines with six stressors (closures, megamorphic shapes, type churn, throw-catch, surviving allocation, long-lived async) and adds five applications including a React-style reconciler, a warm router, a bytecode VM, a hot module graph and the unmodified `nanoid` package. Its first captures on 26 August were 1.111× and 1.029×; `af7289f1` records 0.961×, "UNDER PARITY (first in series)", and the next two days reach 0.937× and 0.920×.

entries.title: Sandbox hardening for untrusted code
entries.summary: The native and WebAssembly sandboxes are hardened for arbitrary hostile input, one day after ARM64 gets its first JIT tier.

blocks.text: `e89612a6` (24 August) hardens the sandboxes and adds the guarded ARM64 baseline JIT: bounded call-free integer functions and numeric loops with exact-ip fallback, no helpers, no OSR yet, and a bespoke W^X path on Windows ARM64. `4195e063` continues the hardening for untrusted code: compile-time `forbid(unsafe_code)` under `safe-sandbox`, a compile error if `safe-sandbox` and `jit` are combined, and separate workspaces so feature unification cannot reintroduce a JIT.

entries.title: Crossing Node parity at 0.9695×
entries.summary: Wave 19 decomposes the three rows that were 60% of the remaining gap on 23 August; the next day the headline ten rows record 0.9695× Node.

blocks.text: `0f1a4c71` (23 August) is "wave 19 -- the three rows nobody had decomposed were 60% of the gap", at 1.0997×. `c6ffa200`, the next day, is "bench: cross Node parity at 0.9695x". Fifty-six days earlier the same suite had been at 4.20×.

entries.title: A tier-differential fuzzer finds five live wrong-answer classes
entries.summary: Running the same programs through the interpreter and every JIT tier and diffing the outputs finds five classes of silent wrong answers.

blocks.text: The engine had already learned this lesson once in June, when an adversarial audit of the JIT found six soundness bugs, and again on 13 June when "the INT tier was silently returning wrong answers on ordinary loops -- a dense-array tag check scratched a live Bool home register". `ee14c71d` makes the check systematic: a fuzzer that runs generated programs in every tier and diffs the results, which found five more classes. A later commit found that "the operand table was blind to 185 of 221 opcodes -- 23 wrong-answer shapes, one root cause".

entries.title: The first capture under 1.20× Node
entries.summary: 1.196× on the headline ten, with typedarray-math reaching Node parity for the first time.

blocks.text: `cdf064c4`: "the wave-13 capture on the PGO build -- 1.2511x -> 1.1962x [1.192, 1.201], the first capture under 1.20x; typedarray-math reaches node parity". The double tier's unboxed register homes are what carried it.

entries.title: The nursery goes default-on
entries.summary: After a two-week pause, the non-moving generational nursery is enabled by default, taking the headline capture from 1.283× to 1.212× Node.

blocks.text: The log had been quiet since 4 August. `74d03d23` is "the nursery goes default-on": minor collections trace young reachability plus remembered old-to-young edges; promotion is a bookkeeping change on the same heap index because the collector never moves objects. The wave-9 capture moved from 1.2832× to 1.2117×. `ZIPP_NO_NURSERY=1` keeps the majors-only mode for conformance runs and ablations.

entries.title: The nursery lands (stage 1 refuted, stage 3 proven); zipp.org goes up
entries.summary: The generational nursery's first stage is refuted by its own measurements before the third stage lands with a prover; the first landing page is committed the same day.

blocks.text: `docs/archive/NURSERY_DESIGN.md` was written when GC looked dominant; the ledger later corrected that ("GC is 2-12%, not dominant — B81 corrected" and "it is the COLLECTOR, not the allocator — pool built, measured zero, reverted"). Stage 1 of the nursery was refuted; stage 3 (`82e454fa`, `72cb640f`) landed with a prover that verifies remembered-set invariants, `ZIPP_NURSERY_VERIFY=1`. The design document now carries a header calling itself historical. `0d124bf1`, "feat: add Zipp landing page", is the first version of this site.

entries.title: PGO adopted at −13.3%
entries.summary: Profile-guided optimization takes the headline from 1.749× to 1.451× Node in one build change; two more waves the same day reach 1.330×.

blocks.text: `5cafcb10`. Every capture since has been a PGO build with the profile's hash, the recipe, the compiler, the linker and the source snapshot all recorded in the artifact; the working rule is "PGO retrain before any headline capture" and "never promote a dirty, filtered, non-PGO, or incomplete-engine artifact".

entries.title: The first capture the repository can attribute to a commit
entries.summary: Benchmark artifacts begin recording engine commit, dirty flag, competitor hashes and per-repetition schedules, after a harness was found able to name a commit it had never measured.

blocks.text: `f1b38086`: "bench: the first capture this repo can attribute to a commit". The sampling profiler the roadmap had wanted since its third ticket landed the day before. The ledger's measurement-hygiene section records the failures that motivated this: a profiler "lying about a quarter of json-large", a harness that "could name a commit it had never measured", and a leftover `ZIPP_GC_STRESS=1` process from a killed session that held a core for hours and was misdiagnosed as an engine livelock.

entries.title: A new home at github.com/f2i-com/zipp.org
entries.summary: The README points at the repository's permanent address; the day before, the corpus refresh had left Test262 at 95,939 of 95,942.

blocks.text: `94e7e0f5` moves the README to the new home. `d5d0ae7b` (29 July) refreshed the corpus and implemented `Iterator.prototype.join`, 36 executions that V8 24.12 does not pass either: "the suite is the oracle, not node". `799ead6d` recorded the last full-suite Intl402 figure on record, 6,502 of 6,714.

entries.title: 30 failures to 5, and 22 of the 30 were runner defects
entries.summary: Two phantom executions removed, then 22 of 30 remaining failures traced to the repository or runner rather than the engine; 99.995% on 95,846 executions.

blocks.text: `a3d616d3` reaches 99.97% with 30 failures and claims Annex B handling "more conformant than Node", a claim later retracted. `d0854919`: "test262: 30 -> 5, and none of the 5 is a live engine defect". Of the five, module-level `using` declarations that were never disposed accounted for six executions fixed the same day, and the mutually exclusive Annex B pair ("95,942/95,942 does not exist for any engine — V8 fails the same one") became the standing caveat.

entries.title: Intl.DurationFormat, the IANA time-zone database, and the Test262 tail
entries.summary: Non-ISO Temporal calendars take Intl402 from 63.6% to 96.9% in a day; the core suite reaches 99.91%.

blocks.text: Four commits in one day: `b550a4ca` adds `Intl.DurationFormat` and the IANA database generated from pinned upstream data; `04edd833` adds non-ISO Temporal calendars (Intl402 63.6% → 85.3%); `1ae58724` reaches 99.88% core and 96.9% Intl402; `f1997ad8` reaches 99.91%. Temporal ended up with fifteen calendars: twelve closed-form, Chinese and Dangi by astronomical calculation, and Umm al-Qura from the required month data.

entries.title: 99.0%, a new in-house front end, and an honest denominator change
entries.summary: A new front end cuts parse-negative failures from 607 files to 80; honouring YAML list-form flags drops the denominator by 181 executions and the score is republished.

blocks.text: `6fc39171` (98.1%) is the new front end built for correct early errors. `321c328b` reaches 99.0% (95,091 of 96,029). `8cec7647` then honours YAML list-form `flags:` metadata, which removes 181 phantom executions and changes the denominator to 95,848; the number was republished as 99.2% rather than left inflated.

entries.title: zipp-wasm: a persistent VM for browser hosts, and fat LTO
entries.summary: The WebAssembly embedding lands as a persistent VM that compiles once and re-enters later; fat LTO with one codegen unit buys about 2%; regex literals validated at compile time add 712 executions.

blocks.text: `f6f4a804` adds `zipp-wasm`; `768287f8` adds the persistent-VM embedding API, "compile once, re-enter later", which is the model the browser `Engine` class still follows. `694886b8` turns on fat LTO and `codegen-units = 1` (2.80× → 2.77×, "free"). `44c4c738` validates regular-expression literals at compile time, the single largest conformance jump of the week at +712 executions.

entries.title: The reckoning: 96.97%, not 100%
entries.summary: After six silent weeks, the Test262 runner is found to have been scoring a single execution mode; the honest pass rate is 96.97%. The same day, every crate but zipp-vm is deleted and the docs are rewritten against measurements.

blocks.text: `1217d683`: "Fix the test262 runner; real pass rate is 96.97%, not 100%". The runner had reported 48,550 passes of 48,556 single-mode executions; the corpus required 96,029. `9ef187f9`: "Focus the workspace on zipp-vm; rewrite the docs against measurements", deleting the AOT, Cranelift, LLVM, zero-knowledge and TypeScript crates from May. `b865f9c6` adopts `mimalloc` as the global allocator, 4.20× → 3.34× Node on the honest suite. The roadmap's B10 entry the same day is "the measured backlog from the 25-agent speed hunt".

related.label: The article: building to Test262 conformance

entries.title: Tier C function JIT on by default, and a checkable roadmap
entries.summary: The whole-function JIT tier is enabled by default (parse 4.1× → 3.3× Node) and docs/PERF_ROADMAP.md is written as a checkable path to V8 parity. Then the log goes quiet for six weeks.

blocks.text: `4e12a406` and `f0d725a8` enable the Tier C function-level JIT by default. `62dbba15` adds `docs/PERF_ROADMAP.md`, whose tickets (B1, B2, B3…) number every later performance commit. The day before, `7e29d967` had fixed six JIT soundness bugs found by an adversarial audit of the session's own codegen. June ends with 1,039 commits.

entries.title: WTF-8 strings, big BigInt, and the honest benchmark pack
entries.summary: Strings gain real lone-surrogate support, BigInt gains a two-tier i128 plus num-bigint implementation, and bench/real arrives as a ten-workload five-engine suite.

blocks.text: `c43b17ce`: WTF-8 so that a lone surrogate survives a round trip, as ECMAScript requires. `7f4e58b6`: BigInt with an `i128` fast tier backed by `num-bigint`. `f00c2010`: "Add bench/real: ten-workload five-engine suite (the honest pack)", the ancestor of today's real13 suite. The day before, `b2c04ace` had given `Atomics` a real blocking wait with a global FIFO waiter registry and cross-thread notify, and `247238ca` had added proper tail calls.

entries.title: ES modules with top-level await
entries.summary: Module mode lands with top-level await and a Test262 module runner; modules become runtime structures on the explicit frame stack like everything else.

blocks.text: `5fba4d7d`: "Run ES modules: top-level-await module mode + test262 module runner". The module graph, `[[CycleRoot]]`, deferred evaluation ordering and errored-cycle re-import would each get their own fix over the following three months; today's `zipp mjs` is the descendant of this commit.

entries.title: eval, the number-one conformance lever, and ShadowRealm
entries.summary: Indirect and global-scope eval land, followed by ShadowRealm, both as runtime structures rather than native recursion.

blocks.text: `76169428`: "implement eval (indirect / global-scope) — the #1 conformance lever". `97e07a67` adds `ShadowRealm`. Both are cheap in an explicit-frame VM: a new realm is a new set of intrinsics and a new global, not a new native stack.

entries.title: RegExp, TypedArrays, Proxy, Temporal and Intl in one day
entries.summary: A forked regress engine for regular expressions, eleven TypedArray constructors, Proxy traps, Temporal type by type, the whole Intl namespace, a mark-sweep GC, and a 17,400-line vm.rs split into a folder.

blocks.text: The busiest day in the log. `8520b6a8` wires regular expressions through the `regress` crate (later forked for UTF-16 execution and a regex JIT). `65e33aed`: `ArrayBuffer` and eleven TypedArray constructors. `48633f27`: Proxy traps. `4a3f85b6` through `00df2adc`: Temporal, from `Duration` to `PlainDate` to `Instant` to `Now`. `ebf7dca3`: "implement the Intl namespace + all 11 services (0 -> ~340 tests)". `a9b1d901`: "split the 17.4k-line vm.rs into a vm/ module folder". `b5d691e1`: a mark-sweep collector for the new VM.

entries.title: A Test262 runner, and async generators as the biggest lever
entries.summary: The conformance runner lands one day after the pivot, and async generators are implemented as the largest single block of failing executions.

blocks.text: `79d10480`: "tools: add test262 conformance runner". `dd820da7`: "async generators (async function*) — the biggest conformance lever". From this day on, features were measured in executions passed, though it would take until 25 July for the runner to count them correctly.

entries.title: First native JIT, inline caches, ropes, and a first win over V8
entries.summary: The register VM gets an x86-64 JIT for hot integer functions, OSR loop regions, call-free inline caches, scalar replacement, rope strings and a microtask loop, and beats V8 on loop.js at 26.5 ms against 28.0.

blocks.text: In one day: `59032ebd` "native x86-64 JIT for hot integer functions (4.1x where it fires)"; `b882eea5` "OSR loop-region JIT (double/SSE2)"; `050fe88d` "call-free inline cache for GetProp/SetProp — object.js 14ms → 3ms"; `bca59c77` scalar replacement, "object 31ms → 8ms"; `e6e63a0a` "rope strings + cached length/index — kill the O(n²) in string concat & scan"; `0db0d5af` "Remove the old JS engines; `zipp js` now runs zipp-vm"; `a5cf5a3e` promises and a microtask event loop; and `d7d9d5e0`, "cheap 2^53 guard (range trick) — BEAT V8 on loop.js (26.5 vs 28.0ms)".

entries.title: The pivot to JavaScript, and the register VM that stuck
entries.summary: The ES5 object model arrives, a bytecode compiler and VM are built, two engines are tried, and by evening the clean-sheet explicit-frame register VM exists. So does the first retraction of a false performance claim.

blocks.text: `262ae969`: "prototypes, `new`, `instanceof`, `in` (the ES5 object model)". `e2440724` wires `zipp js <file.js>`. A fuzzer campaign follows, fixing `Number::toString` and bugs numbered 1 through 32 one commit at a time. `ecc96a94` is the first bytecode compiler and VM; `4c826c54` absorbs an earlier engine and rebrands it; `50634ccd` is "FIX broken build + RETRACT the false perf claims in 4c826c5". Then `87174f64`: "zipp-vm: clean-sheet JS engine v2 — explicit-frame register VM", the design every later page on this site describes.

entries.title: Day one: ZIPP language v0, with four back ends before midnight
entries.summary: The initial commit is a tree-walking interpreter for a small typed language; by the end of the day it has a Cranelift JIT, an LLVM tier, a mark-sweep GC, a gas-metered WebAssembly profile, a zero-knowledge back end and a TypeScript front end.

blocks.text: `a71a1bdc`, "Initial commit - ZIPP language v0", 13:38 on 29 May 2026. `d0fe82fa`: "Add native JIT (Cranelift) for the integer subset — beats V8 on a hot loop". `c30bb934`: "Add LLVM release tier (clang -O3) — matches V8 on dense f64". `924ed4a1`: a conservative mark-sweep GC. `fe045b2b`: "the WASM contract profile: deterministic, gas-metered WebAssembly". `b1847a67`: "zk hardening: bind proofs to a program hash". `5d1c1fab`: a TypeScript front end via `oxc`. All of it was deleted on 25 July; the habit of naming the measurement in the commit subject survived.

entries.title: A language model from its GGUF file, and weights that stay quantized
entries.summary: An experimental local-model plugin overlay arrives, and the GPU protocol learns to keep a checkpoint's Q4_K and Q6_K blocks and decode them inside the matmul on every backend.

blocks.text: `277f30fa` applies a local-model Python plugin overlay verbatim, checked against its own `SHA256SUMS`, and says plainly that its integration gates had never run. The rest of the day made it real. `90e0a9c7` and `9472d78f` gave the Python frontend relative imports and a no-op `torch.autocast`, which with 341 lines of shim was enough for Hugging Face's Qwen3, Qwen2, Llama and Mistral modelling files to run exactly as published, within 2e-7 of transformers. The commit makes a point worth keeping: what stood in the way was never numpy, but four tensor operations, autocast, relative imports and those 341 lines.

`379a04cc` reads GGUF without holding the file: a 6.8 GB checkpoint opens in 35 ms from a 16 MiB header read. `ad64fce3` is the decision that matters: a Q4_K weight is 144 bytes per 256 values and 1,024 once expanded, so an `input` may now carry `q4_k` or `q6_k` blocks and every backend decodes them inside a `transposed` matmul, held to bit-for-bit equality with the same matmul over decoded values. `e6c33be3` made the browser side Rust, `6f847191` added a Qwen3 plugin that reads the checkpoint where it lies, and by the evening `03b5c283` moved the container, block formats and tokenizer out to their own project, [gguf-wasm](https://github.com/f2i-com/gguf-wasm), keeping only what is ZIPP's: the kernels and the protocol.

entries.title: A model in stages, a product in integers, and v0.0.20
entries.summary: Qwen3 splits into stages that reproduce the whole model bit for bit, matmul_fixed accumulates in integers so every backend gives the same bits, the kernels build reproducibly, and v0.0.20 ships.

blocks.text: Every quantized test until then compared ZIPP with ZIPP. `e8053573` compares the whole chain with transformers reading the same GGUF, an implementation that shares nothing with it: the worst of 455,808 logits differs by 7.4e-5. `50ec6a98` then ran Qwen3 as two stages with a hidden state crossing between them and got the whole model's logits bit for bit, and `d7fe124e` put the stages in worker threads and killed one, measuring that a restarted stage is not recovery: it differs in 151,936 of 151,936 logits and predicts " the" where the model says " Paris".

`c4409b6f` adds `matmul_fixed`: both sides quantized to int16 against their own row's maximum and summed as integers, so the answer is the same bits on every backend by construction rather than by agreeing on rounding order, which is what a proof system over a prime field needs. WebGPU and WebGL2 have no 64-bit integer to accumulate in, so they refuse the graph; before this, an operation a backend had no kernel for returned a buffer of zeros. `435ea899` runs a prompt 16 positions at a time into the same caches, 65 ms a token against 182, bit for bit. `fdc639c5` made `kernels.wasm` build to the same bytes on Windows and Linux and has CI rebuild and compare it, and [v0.0.20](https://github.com/f2i-com/zipp.org/releases/tag/v0.0.20) was published with the plugins source only.

entries.title: Fixes first: the model host, the host boundary and the Python frontend
entries.summary: Before building further, a pass over the model host, gpu-lab sessions, the WebAssembly host boundary, the dev server, the Python frontend and the JIT fixes the defects found, each with a regression test.

blocks.text: The round began with fixes rather than features. The GPT-Neo tokenizer skipped every merge line starting with `#`, not just the header, dropping eight real merges (`787b73a3`). A gpu-lab session accepted a float feed for a quantized input and handed the floats to the backends as block bytes, and the WebAssembly arena never gave back what sessions pinned (`dfbd51bb`). `zipp run --bc a.js` executed the script it was asked only to print (`4ec0f002`). On Windows the dev server served `.git/config` through its 8.3 short name `/GIT~1/config` (`d80f2d91`). A host object key with a lone surrogate merged two keys and dropped a value without error (`a04da81a`).

`f2ba827d` fixed the Python frontend against CPython 3.11 and PyTorch 2.11: a generator suspended inside `except` leaked its exception into the caller, exact ties in `e` and `g` formats rounded away from zero, argparse hung on any `store_true` flag, and `torch.save` wrote a global PyTorch cannot load. `17cb442a` fixed a JIT wrap that changed results: once compiled, `(a + b + 0.5) | 0` at `a = 2^31-1, b = 1` gave -2147483647 instead of -2147483648.

entries.title: The torch layer, checked against PyTorch 2.11
entries.summary: Silent errors in eager torch are fixed, the layers, optimizers, dtypes, linalg, fft and distributions ordinary training code uses are added, and eager torch's heavy loops run natively: about 4.8x faster, same bytes.

blocks.text: The commits lead with what was silently wrong. In-place arithmetic rebound a tensor to new storage, so the textbook `w.data.add_(w.grad, alpha=-lr)` left the weights unchanged; float32 means accumulated in float32, so the mean of a million 0.1s was 0.100958 (`1f95d6f9`). The -100 padding label indexed a real class and a reassigned BatchNorm buffer never reached `state_dict` (`cfc8e990`). A PyTorch Adam checkpoint drifted its bias correction (`782cc0aa`), and `torch.compile` training captured an eager op on a parameter as a new leaf whose gradient never reached it (`7dd1db31`). Each fix is checked against values PyTorch 2.11 generated, and each commit adds what training code reaches for: about 200 tensor functions, the common layers, 12 optimizers, 15 schedulers, `torch.utils.data`, float16 and bfloat16 (stored in two bytes by `61b960e5`), `torch.linalg` and `torch.distributions`.

Speed came second and without changing a byte. `14a2ef71` turned the JIT on for `zipp py` and `fb5ecc0a` reverted it the same night, because once the tensor loops ran natively the JIT made training slower. `b24c6b81` is that change: matmul, convolution, elementwise ops and reductions run as Rust natives that repeat the JavaScript's float64 operations in the same order, and 20,828 native-against-JavaScript cases differ in no byte. `torch_matmul` went from 319 to 8.4 ms and the geometric mean to 0.21× its time. `2481bb47` did the same for `torch.linalg` (a 64x64 `eig` from 218 s to 2.6 ms) and added complex tensors and `torch.fft`.

entries.title: torch.compile on a hardware GPU, natively
entries.summary: Graph protocol versions 3 and 4 add masks, dropout, slicing and gathers bit for bit on five backends, and zipp py runs the same graphs on Vulkan, Direct3D 12 or Metal through wgpu.

blocks.text: `84ccf248` added protocol version 3: `maximum`, `minimum`, comparisons as masks, `where`, and a `uniform` draw computed as a counter hash in 32-bit integers so every backend draws the same bits, which gave `torch.compile` clamping, masking and dropout. ANGLE on Direct3D 11 lost a tied zero's sign in `x < y ? y : x`, so the shaders decide ties first. `eb81d583` added version 4, slicing, `index_select`, `gather` and their gradients, with the protocol fixing the accumulation order so a repeated token's embedding gradient is the same bits everywhere. All five backends agree bit for bit: 276 of 276 cases on WebGPU, WebGL2, WebAssembly and JavaScript, and the references.

`7e2434e5` runs those graphs natively. A new crate, `zipp-gpu`, runs gpu-lab's JavaScript runtime unchanged in a second, trusted Zipp state over a WebGPU shim backed by wgpu, loaded at run time, so no SDK is needed to build and the binary runs anywhere. It is synchronous like the CPU evaluator, so a program's output does not depend on whether a GPU is present. For a 784-2048-2048-10 Adam step at batch 1024 on an RTX 5090, a prepared step took 23.6 ms, against about 25 minutes per call on the CPU evaluator.

entries.title: Python from 22x CPython's time to about 2x
entries.summary: Direct calls, fused Python-only instructions, native helpers, a JIT tier for hot loops, per-VM caches and small integers in the value word take the Python benchmark suite from 22.3x CPython 3.13 to about 2.1x.

blocks.text: The starting point, measured on the `tools/python_bench.py` suite against CPython 3.13: 22.3× its time. `f9347730` took it to 8.55× with a new calling convention, per-class inline caches and ten fused Python-only instructions executed out of line so the JavaScript interpreter loop is unchanged. `771eba6b` added seventeen more and native `json`, string, `heapq` and `bisect` helpers, to 5.3×. `cff586d2` gave the command line a JIT tier for hot Python loops; every fused instruction it does not inline calls the interpreter's own step and continues where that step chose, so results are identical. `d6bf5cf0`, `6ff55c9f` and `2b5e2028` made exceptions, generators and lookups cheaper, to 3.6× with the JIT.

`fd18aaf7` was the big step. Python's `int` is a BigInt in the runtime, so integer code allocated on every operation. A BigInt within ±2^46 is now an immediate in the value word, reusing the null tag's bit pattern with payload bit 47 set, so no new tag was needed and every existing is-a-double check stayed valid. The geometric mean with the JIT fell from 3.6× to 2.1×, and `range_loop`, `int_arith`, `float_arith`, `tuple_swap` and `global_read` beat CPython. JavaScript BigInt code got 2-4× faster, other JavaScript is unchanged, and Test262 passes as before.

entries.title: Torch as a package, and a GPU step under PyTorch's eager CUDA
entries.summary: Python without torch becomes a smaller WebAssembly variant with torch as a verified package, the Python parser becomes hand-written and then Zipp's own, and a prepared GPU step falls to 0.27 ms against PyTorch's 0.78.

blocks.text: The torch work had made the Python module heavy, so this day took weight out. `eb2baa1e` embeds the Python library comment-stripped, token for token (57 KB smaller on the wire). `76a1f721` replaced the vendored parser's generated tables with a hand-written recursive-descent parser checked over 1.3 million mutated token streams, and `c112164c` replaced that with Zipp's own front end, `zipp-pyparse`. `7ee10b51` compiles bundled modules on first import, so a program that imports torch in the browser starts in about 300 ms instead of 560. `8e9e5d2e` split torch out: the `python` variant is 1.68 MB on the wire, below 0.0.20's 1.71 MB, and `zipp_torch.wasm` (0.38 MB) adds torch at run time after the engine checks its format, ABI hash and every file's SHA-256.

On the native GPU, `c3b1c38f` replays a prepared step's recorded command list itself, one submit and one readback per run. `8ceb6f91` took a small MLP's step from 0.94 to 0.53 ms, under PyTorch's eager CUDA on the same RTX 5090. `f6254f56` fuses kernels only where each element's arithmetic is unchanged and adds a 128x128 matmul tile (48 TFLOP/s on a 4096³ product), and `45764899` sends steps in binary and cuts a small step to 12 dispatches: 0.27 ms, 0.12 ms at eight per run, against 0.78 ms for PyTorch's eager CUDA and 0.17 ms for its CUDA graph, bit for bit the same on Vulkan, Direct3D 12 and Chrome. `eaeab1f3` stopped a `dxcompiler.dll` on PATH from silently changing Direct3D 12's float results.

entries.title: Python at 1.75x CPython, own parser only, and v0.0.21
entries.summary: Native dict, set and instance storage, direct calls and inlined attribute access take Python to about 1.75x CPython 3.13 with the JIT; a hello-world starts in 20 ms; the compiler reads Zipp's own syntax tree and emits the same bytecode every run.

blocks.text: Most of a `zipp py` hello-world's 85 ms went into compiling the 0.7 MB Python runtime in every process. `9ad9c7bb` caches compiled code per user, keyed on the executable, the source and every `ZIPP_*` setting, so a warm hello-world takes about 20 ms (CPython: 15-20). Embedding a precompiled snapshot in the WebAssembly module was measured and rejected, since it would more than double the runtime's share of the download; the browser calls `prewarmPython()` when idle instead, and the first run takes about 20 ms instead of 220.

`50e490b0` moves dicts and sets into a native compact table modelled on CPython 3.13's, `65184f04` drops the per-call traceback handler for an ip-to-line table, `74a41f5a` adds `PyCall`, and `4b068438` gives instances hidden-class layouts, which `f954857c` lets compiled loops read and write inline: `attr_read_write` from 19.8 to 3.5 ms, and the suite from about 1.85× to 1.75× CPython's time. One regression was caught on the way: a recycled string slot could satisfy a stale attribute cache, so in torch's backward pass `p._pg` came back as another tensor's list (`444ba261`). `b287409c` prints CPython's traceback layout, and 38 of 44 traceback programs match CPython byte for byte.

`cb3c5bb4` compiles Python from `zipp-pyparse`'s arena tree directly, byte-identical over 61,885 programs, and deletes the RustPython parser fork. `e0af009e` found seven compiler loops that walked a hash set in whatever order the process produced; across 53,673 files the old compiler varied on 139-151 per run and the new one on none. `9df6e2fd` kept the complex power corpus independent of the platform's libm after a last-bit difference on Linux, and [v0.0.21](https://github.com/f2i-com/zipp.org/releases/tag/v0.0.21) shipped the same day, with torch as a separate WebAssembly package beside the complete engine.

entries.title: ZIPP Lite, and an application bridge for hosts
entries.summary: Hosts can answer application-defined synchronous calls through an app bridge, and ZIPP Lite arrives: the JavaScript core without Intl and Temporal, built for size first.

blocks.text: `13c33194` lets a host answer application-defined synchronous calls through an app bridge, merged with dependency updates as the repository's third pull request (#31). `065446f2` adds ZIPP Lite, a JavaScript-only WebAssembly build without `Intl` and `Temporal`, compiled for size rather than speed, and compacts tables every engine shares.

The commits after it trim Lite's bytecode, its regex duplication, cold error paths, metering and constructor cloning, and the WebAssembly loader's overhead, each with a measured speed check beside the size it saves (`76045145`, `6b854cdc`, `40453bf5`, `85885bb6`, `51187ea6`, `ec0839ce`).

entries.title: Member calls fast again, and compact Unicode tables
entries.summary: The native tiers serve the member calls the strict call order split apart, taking 11% off the 13 native rows; Unicode normalization moves to compact tables, and zipp py opens project files lazily.

blocks.text: Making specification-order method calls the default in v0.0.15 split a member call into a property read, the arguments and a call, and the native tiers had stopped serving the split form. `739603bc` serves Map, Set, string and `hasOwn.call` member calls through their intrinsic helpers again, `5c046753` caches a Map or Set method read in the native inline cache, and `d91ae358` answers `.length` from the internal slot: the 13 real rows take 10.95% less time, and the headline ten were at 0.982× Node 24 in an ordinary release build. `131aa66c` delay-loads the GPU runtime's system DLLs, so the Windows CLI starts in 6.3 ms instead of 8.9.

The size passes went on beside it. `0fb24b41` builds WebAssembly without machine paths and runs `wasm-opt -O1` twice; `9df8019c` replaces the `unicode-normalization` crate's hashed tables with ranked bitmaps, and `ba63d8a0` packs the regex properties of strings into one pool: the four modules came out 1.6% to 4.4% smaller after Brotli. `ee34f2cb` reads a Python project's files only when the program opens them (a script run from this repository's root starts in 62 ms instead of 460), `8d909598` bounds the code cache, and `5253e4e0` leaves a finished program's heap to the process's exit.

entries.title: The WebAssembly interpreter profiled, and v0.0.22
entries.summary: A first profile of the WebAssembly modules makes four quadratic string workloads linear, Lite stops making every register access a call, and v0.0.22 ships with ZIPP Lite as an asset.

blocks.text: The twelfth size pass profiled the modules for the first time. The checked profile now keeps a well-formed string's bytes as text (`4e8cb084`), flattens a rope before a RegExp exec (`58735a8a`), counts a compiled RegExp program toward the collection trigger (`76420e1f`) and shares the UTF-16 and UCS-2 regex matchers in every module (`13b56e42`): the JavaScript corpus takes 0.90 of the time, a sticky-regex tokenizer over 190 KB 164 ms instead of 17.8 s, and a loop that built and dropped large RegExps no longer dies of uncollected programs.

The thirteenth made a Lite register access one bounds check instead of a call, which had been 38% of an integer loop (`09bf2c18`), so Lite runs its corpus in 0.61 of the time; shares the Python runtime's compiled functions between programs instead of copying them (`4a5dc9ac`); and stops copying the value of a statement nobody reads (`7190396a`). Two update-expression bugs were fixed in every build: `k++` on a `const` local changed the constant before throwing, and `f++` inside `function f` replaced the function (`cc074ade`). [v0.0.22](https://github.com/f2i-com/zipp.org/releases/tag/v0.0.22) was published from `4a9a9124` on 10 October with modules 11% to 15% smaller than v0.0.21's, and ZIPP Lite joined it as a seventh asset the same day (`18a8d935`).

entries.title: Memory grown in place, compiled callbacks, and v0.0.23
entries.summary: Memory that grows in place reaches the collector, an appending loop stops rewriting typeof's strings, builtins call compiled functions without the interpreter loop, and v0.0.23 ships with Python at 1.30x CPython.

blocks.text: Seven wrong results in v0.0.22 were found and fixed. The largest: memory that grows in place (an array pushed to a megabyte, an object gathering thousands of keys, a filling Map) allocates no new object, so a loop that built and dropped such things ran no collection; a browser engine ended the script at its heap ceiling, and natively 2,000 calls that each built an 80,000-element array held 1.2 GB. `d24fe3e8` reads what the allocator has outstanding and collects on that growth, and the same program peaks at 60 MB. `dcbfe67d` stops `var s = "number"; s += x` from rewriting the string `typeof` returns, and `20123116` unwraps a chain of bound functions in a loop instead of by recursion.

On speed, `784e3eb2` and `1ba123a5` let builtins enter a compiled callback without the interpreter loop: six million capturing `map` and `forEach` callbacks take 79 ms where they took 232 (Node: 64). `54a63349` steps a generator in `for-of` without its result object, `649595f8` compiles `new` in memory regions and Tier C bodies, and `8b9b25c5` predicts a keyed access's slot from the receiver's shape and the key. Python went from 1.79× to 1.30× CPython 3.13, through small-int arithmetic settled in the dispatch loop (`621f798b`), callee frames pushed from the call site's cache (`60d7e502`) and a raise caught in its own frame (`2b217ea4`). [v0.0.23](https://github.com/f2i-com/zipp.org/releases/tag/v0.0.23) shipped on 12 October.

entries.title: Compiled loops for the rest of JavaScript
entries.summary: Loops that build literals, create closures, destructure, spread, pop or hold a for-of compile now, with rest and arguments functions and the Object statics; construction and Object.assign run several times faster.

blocks.text: A compiled loop declined whole when it held one instruction it had no arm for, and fell back to the interpreter. The sixteenth pass gave most of the remaining ones an arm, each through a helper that runs the interpreter's own code for the instruction: literals and `instanceof` and `typeof` tests (`4515054f`), closures (`ebfb8db1`), `pop` (`496e23b8`), destructuring, spread and spread calls (`054f54d4`), key lists and `for-in` (`175e7299`), then `for-of`, a `finally` and array constructors (`85e8bd43`). Functions with a rest parameter or that use `arguments` compile in Tier C (`3a42a658`), and so does code calling `Object.assign`, `String.fromCharCode`, the Promise combinators and the other statics (`1e836768`).

Construction got its own work: a constructor that only stores its arguments builds its object the way a literal is built (`9470f615`), and a compiled loop calls a compiled function without a frame (`8d363095`). Against v0.0.23, two million `new Vec(i, 1)` take 100 ms instead of 760, a million `Object.assign({}, src)` 140 ms instead of 830 (`e9e314f7` copies a plain source directly), and `async-promise-chain`, 1.14× Node at the start of the pass, 0.94×. The 13 native rows take 2.6% less time overall, and the headline ten run at 0.88× Node 24's time with Zipp's median below Node's on every row.

entries.title: Python at 1.09× CPython, torch at 4.2× PyTorch
entries.summary: Python on the command line runs at 1.09x CPython 3.13 with fifteen programs faster than CPython, and torch training and tensor programs at 4.2x PyTorch's warm time, from 17x.

blocks.text: A store-only `__init__` now runs without its frame (`0c0fb3b5`), method lookups and construction sites answer inline for the class they last saw (`8519dc28`), sort keys of one form sort by columns (`93fac141`), a subscript reads a list's, tuple's or dict's record once (`e7153c9f`), `raise` has a compiled helper (`a3476e76`), and loops are planned only where the header dominates the back edge (`c5374b88`). Over the 36 programs Python runs at 1.09× CPython 3.13's time, from 1.31× at v0.0.23; the 30 small programs are level with CPython, and fifteen programs beat it. `05704850` fixed a zero-argument `super()` beside a lambda or inside a comprehension, and `79759baa` won back 5% on every interpreted Python call after a dispatch-loop change had cost it.

Torch draws its random numbers natively (`ce8e1494`) and `uniform_` now rounds as PyTorch does (`832c3756`); add, sub, mul, div and the common matrix products are one engine call (`4c2c8ed2`, `69471503`), and powers are computed the way PyTorch's kernel computes them (`10d8465e`). On one thread, warm, eight training and tensor programs take 4.2× PyTorch 2.11's time, where v0.0.23 took 17×, and a program's first run is faster than PyTorch's on four of them.

entries.title: Eight reported bugs fixed, and v0.0.24
entries.summary: The repository's first eight GitHub issues, from typed-array own indices to a derived class's newTarget.prototype, are fixed with tests and answered, and v0.0.24 ships with smaller WebAssembly engines.

blocks.text: The repository's first eight GitHub issues came from @takahashim, each with a minimal repro and a pointer into the source: a typed array's in-range indices were not own properties (#32, `8ce16ff8`); a function's `prototype` made non-writable stayed writable (#33, `5980d5a7`); `obj.hasOwnProperty(k)` ran the built-in for any receiver, skipping a Proxy's traps (#34, `861cda39`); a class on a function's prototype chain was walked past (#41, `acca1331`); `typeof name` inside `with` read the global (#42, `2ba3b5a0`); a replaced `console` method was never called, and there was no `performance` object (#43 and #44, `6333c421`, `f229dc1c`); and a derived construction read `newTarget.prototype` itself (#45, `18643638`). Each fix was checked against Node 24 with the JIT on and off and under GC stress, and pinned by a test.

Differential programs found more: a global redefined with `Object.defineProperty(globalThis, …)` went on being called as the old function by a compiled loop (`ea1a9d8b`), `arguments.length = n` deleted elements, and `toLocaleLowerCase` in Turkish, Azerbaijani and Lithuanian missed the final sigma. The gates caught two regressions of the pass's own before release: a 5% cost on every interpreted Python call, and a compiled-loop optimization lost to the `console.log` change (`35e6d1dc`). [v0.0.24](https://github.com/f2i-com/zipp.org/releases/tag/v0.0.24) was published on 14 October from `a82ad0bb`; its browser modules are 1.0% to 4.0% smaller on the wire than v0.0.23's, the JavaScript-only module 1.13 MB and ZIPP Lite 0.67 MB.

entries.title: Ten reported embedding bugs fixed, and v0.0.25
entries.summary: Ten more issues from @takahashim, from a Proxy on the global object's prototype chain to a heap ceiling a VM could not recover from, are fixed, and v0.0.25's safe-sandbox interpreter runs the benchmark rows in 0.84× Bellard's QuickJS's time.

blocks.text: @takahashim embeds Zipp the way a browser-like host does: the safe-sandbox profile with limits on, every script through `eval_in_context`, a Proxy on the global object's prototype chain, wrappers kept in WeakMaps. Their ten reports after v0.0.24 each came with a minimal repro: builtin writes and sloppy unresolvable assignments that went to that Proxy (#46 and #47, `5762df5a`); a promise's resolving functions that were not function objects (#48, `6efdad8c`); `WeakMap#delete` rebuilding its index (#49, `bdd7538f`); global reads slowing down as a realm grew, and a builtin reassigned on the global object (#50 and #51, `cbea93aa`, `476de138`); a function that merely named `eval` (#52, `5f2bf15d`); code from `new Function` and `eval` never freed (#53, `9c7d1a54`, `5bd3ac46`); a top-level `let` that the fix for #47 had broken on `main` (#54, `476de138`); and a VM that could not allocate again after reaching its heap ceiling (#55, `ca0091bc`).

The same embedding set the performance work beside the fixes. Against v0.0.24, the safe-sandbox profile runs the 13 benchmark rows in 0.58× the time, 0.84× Bellard's QuickJS's and 0.53× QuickJS-NG's, with about half the peak memory. Running #50's own program in that profile turned up one more defect before release: it held only 1,024 globals created at run time, now 16,384 (`3e8a5d07`). [v0.0.25](https://github.com/f2i-com/zipp.org/releases/tag/v0.0.25) was published on 15 October from `ddbd0272`.

entries.title: Property caches inline, sorts without calls, and an eval fix
entries.summary: After v0.0.25: the hostile bytecode-vm row back from 170 to 49 ms, a property cache's own-data hit taken inline in the interpreter, sorts and bitwise array callbacks without a call per element, and eval code that sees a replaced builtin.

blocks.text: The 15 October capture had the hostile `bytecode-vm` row at 3.13× Node's time, from 0.98× on 2 September. Since the strict call order, its helper-table loop needed nine spill slots where a compiled integer region may use eight, so the whole loop fell to the slowest tier; a region holding a computed-call splice may now spill up to twelve (`fdb0222f`), and the row runs in 49 ms instead of 170. In the interpreter, a property cache's own-data read and store are taken inline instead of through the full cache call (`082d4a21`, `bdbec963`), which moved the 18-row interpreter geomean against Bellard's QuickJS from 0.903× to 0.866×. A sort by the exact comparator `(x, y) => x - y` over Numbers computes each comparison without calling it in every unmetered profile (`d9290e55`; 200,000 Numbers in 18 ms instead of 90, interpreted), the fused map, filter and reduce kernels learned the bitwise operators (`95fbe2dd`), a compiled `Map.get` went from 24 to 14 ns (`df840d75`, `879d7cf8`), and narrowing a double to an int and DataView member calls got cheaper (`fc54b5a9`, `786be5b4`).

One wrong result came from the same embedding style as v0.0.25's reports: a program that silenced `print` with `globalThis.print = function () {}` still printed from `eval`, indirect eval, `new Function` and an embedder's later scripts, because code compiled after the program started seeded its slot with the original builtin. The slot now takes the builtin only while the global object still holds it, and the first write of a builtin through the global object keeps its non-enumerable attributes, as OrdinarySet does (`b628f56d`). `a34c60e6` pins those writes on a non-extensible, a frozen and a sealed global against Node.

entries.title: Torch kernels in native loops, and Python allocation trimmed
entries.summary: Torch matrix products use AVX2 when the CPU has it, slice stores and index gradients run in native loops, short-lived tensor buffers are reclaimed by minor collections, and Python strings and instances recycle their buffers.

blocks.text: When the CPU has AVX2, `pt_matmul` multiplies four rows by eight columns at a time in four-lane registers, fusing the multiply and add only where every product is exact in an f64, so no value changes (`8a602902`; `torch_matmul` 0.72 ms instead of 0.91). Two element loops in tensor.js were 17% of the instructions a transformer training step ran: the store behind a slice assignment and the accumulation behind an index gather's gradient. Both now try a native loop first (`4775d646`; a 512 × 512 slice store into every other column in 0.28 ms instead of 3.5). TypedArray `fill` and cross-kind `set` store in bulk (`5cc98944`), `x.__class__` is read natively instead of through an interpreted `getattr` call (`d718caa9`), and installed code answers its cache and JIT eligibility without a range search (`fea13f06`).

The collector requested a major collection for every 8 MiB of large payloads, on the belief that the nursery pretenured them. It does not: tensor buffers are born young and die young. The schedule now asks for a minor and makes every fourth one a major (`ec5d4f4c`), and `torch_transformer` at 44 steps took 1 major and 12 minors in 16.2 ms where it took 6 majors and 2 minors in 28.7. The heap also recycles a dead Python instance's attribute buffer (`38d627e0`; 240,000 instances make 122,381 allocations instead of 335,620) and small string buffers for the str methods' results (`3ca7f378`), a literal's keys borrow their site's plan instead of counting references to it (`883dc185`), and a method site keeps the method itself in its cache entry (`b12ce570`). Each change was measured against its parent, mostly a few percent at a time, with the Python suites passing.

entries.title: Superinstructions and a second, smaller interpreter loop
entries.summary: The interpreter runs common instruction pairs as one dispatch, pushes and pops the common frame inline, and runs simple functions and loops in a small second loop that keeps its state in registers.

blocks.text: The first attempt was reverted the same day. Dropping a discarded assignment's result copy whenever the JIT was off (`330a9118`) made a metered program charge different steps with the JIT off than with it on, and the CI-full test that pins that parity failed (`98b4d769`). A JIT-capable build compiles the same bytecode in both modes again, and interpreter-only rewrites now go into a copy of each function's code instead. That copy is `b2b8f5ca`'s: adjacent pairs such as a loop bound's load and compare-branch, `x + 1`, or a counter step and its back-edge run as one superinstruction, while the original instructions stay in place for jumps, inline caches, the JIT and every recorder. `1b04c9bb` pushes and pops the common frame inline, and `af87a2c7` moved the choice of the copy past the native tiers, which had cost a JIT row about 7%.

`702ad388` adds `vm/lite.rs`, a second interpreter loop small enough to keep its state in registers, for functions made only of loads, adds, compare-branches, calls and returns; it works on the real frames, so handing an instruction back to the main loop is free. `11c60356` then stopped re-checking the register file's live prefix on every read and write, a check the PC profile showed before each register write of `fib`. Later commits let the lite loop run loops with cached property and element access (`d0a110be`) and closures and Math methods (`4c16fc70`), and compiled it twice so a small copy keeps recursive integer functions fast (`a2e02db3`). In the commits' profile-guided measurements against Bellard's QuickJS 2026-06-04, the 18-row interpreter geomean went from 0.681× to 0.630× with the superinstructions and inline frames, and to 0.576× after the register-file change, faster on 16 of 18 rows; [the expansion suite's entry](/journal/twenty-one-new-workloads-against-quickjs/) explains why the held-out recipe's numbers are the ones to quote. Module namespaces also moved from SipHash to FxHash (`16034c8c`; `module-hot-graph` in 0.78× its previous time, interpreted).

entries.title: One folder per language, and a table of languages
entries.summary: Each language's parser, compiler, runtime and native tier now live under src/lang/, a language is one entry of a table, docs/LANGUAGES.md describes how a language plugs into the shared VM, and the documentation moves under docs/.

blocks.text: JavaScript's parser and compiler sat at the top of `src/`, and Python was spread across `frontend/python`, `vm/py_*.rs`, `codegen/` and `vm/engine/`. `da8427b6` gathers each language under `src/lang/`: `lang/js/` holds the parser, the compiler and the front end, and `lang/python/` the frontend, its runtime and bundled library, its VM side and its native tier. Only files moved. Every module kept its name and its place in the module tree, so no item, symbol or visibility changed; `f89d51b8` fixed the one path the torch package's build still spelled the old way, and `06164d14` moved the Python parser crate under `lang/python/parser/`, still a crate of its own.

`3c39f3a8` makes a language one entry of a table. A `Language` has its names, file extensions, shebang commands, a single-file compile and its bytecode dump, and detection, `--lang` and the compile dispatch all go through `languages()`, the base language first. [docs/LANGUAGES.md](https://github.com/f2i-com/zipp.org/blob/main/docs/LANGUAGES.md) describes the model it serves: the base instruction set is JavaScript's, a language emits its own instructions where its semantics differ (Python's `Instr::Py*`) and the base ones where they agree, and the document lists the steps for adding a language and the rules every language keeps. The same day the root's working documents moved under `docs/`, with an index and an archive of the dated records (`9f6dd66b`), and 425 old benchmark captures became rows of CSV files in `bench/history/` (`6c2bf933`).

entries.title: Twenty-one new workloads against Bellard's QuickJS
entries.summary: A diagnostic expansion suite of 21 workloads, run with the hostile suite against QuickJS, found where Zipp's interpreter still loses; Proxy traps, private names, Unicode strings, number formatting and eval were the first fixes.

blocks.text: The canonical suites cover 35 workloads. `37da4030` adds `bench/expansion/`, a separate, versioned series of 21 deterministic workloads for what they do not reach: regex compilation, string building and Unicode scanning, small JSON messages, Proxy and accessors, objects as dictionaries, private class members, generators, a DataView codec, `new Function` and eval, and more. Every case prints byte-identical output on Node 24, Zipp and QuickJS at three sizes, and the harness records process cycles and peak memory and reports each row with a bootstrap interval. The first record (`46f8cafe`) needed a correction the same day: its build came from an ad-hoc profile-guided recipe trained on the rows it measured, so `a638d95a` added the canonical, held-out recipe's numbers as the ones to quote. Against QuickJS those are 0.674× its time on real13, 0.666× on micro5 and 0.834× on hostile17, and 1.199× on the expansion suite at its medium size, where QuickJS was faster on 14 of the 21 workloads.

The weaknesses the record ranked became the next commits, each checked against Node and timed against QuickJS: dictionary deletes and key probes (`c6b1354a`); Proxy traps that built descriptor objects on every call (`9eed4926`; a forwarding store's get, set and has traps in 154 ms instead of 336, QuickJS 40); private names resolved once per access site (`33e3d1be`); positions in long non-ASCII strings found in bounded time and case maps done in one pass (`93850fc6`, `cccb86d1`), which took the Unicode scanning workload from 374 to 176 ms against QuickJS's 192; a repeated declaration-free direct eval re-run instead of compiled again (`44abf49c`; 27 ms instead of 165, QuickJS 65); `toFixed` and its siblings rounded exactly without guard digits (`07b09f9c`); and `yield*` stepping a generator directly (`86088292`). `0ecf155e` fixed a real bug found on the way: a class member with a computed key had no private brand chain, so it accepted another evaluation's private names where it must throw a TypeError.

entries.title: Dictionary holes, one-dispatch switches and direct statics
entries.summary: Deleting from a large dictionary leaves a hole instead of shifting every later slot, a switch case on a literal dispatches once, and f.call, class statics, WeakMap methods and private fields skip the general paths.

blocks.text: `delete` removed a property's slot with `Vec::remove` and renumbered every slot above it in both indexes, so emptying a 2,100-key dictionary key by key was quadratic. In a map of at least 32 slots the slot now stays as a hole, and holes are compacted in one pass once they are half the slots (`944169e5`). Every reader that walks slots has to skip them, which meant converting about 300 sites by meaning, and the suites were also run with a hole left by every delete to reach them all. Dict-churn's delete phase takes 15 ms instead of 56 (QuickJS 9). A `switch` case on an integer or string literal now runs its load, `===` and branch as one superinstruction (`5793b4c8`; a 15-case integer switch in 87 ms instead of 133, QuickJS 95), and `if (m === 0)` does the same with the other branch sense (`47c13227`).

The rest of the day took general paths out of common calls. `f.call(t, ...)` enters `f` as a frame of the same loop rather than through the builtin dispatcher (`894a1ba9`; a million calls in 30 ms instead of 50, level with QuickJS); class statics and a function's own properties are read and written without the member walk (`4d498c5c`; two million `A.count++` in 44 ms instead of 97); a WeakMap's methods are called directly (`3e9df5d9`); private field reads and writes skip a brand check the field lookup already answers (`e789a836`, `c97d6247`); a Proxy read goes straight to its `[[Get]]` and a forwarded `Reflect.set` stores into the slot (`66bccdb4`, `5d012480`); a typed array's default species view skips the constructor reads (`9fa097ec`); a key added by `o[k] = v` is hashed once (`35f73b1a`); and a present element of a plain array is stored directly (`8ec943a0`). Writing the tests for the class-static lanes found three integrity bugs, fixed in `5f86d140`: `Object.freeze` of a class left its statics writable, a non-extensible class still took new statics, and assigning to a function's own accessor overwrote the getter instead of calling the setter.

entries.title: The latest Test262, run once and unmodified
entries.summary: The Test262 pin moves to tc39/test262 d53ebc8b of 13 October 2026, with iterator chunks, windows and includes, Promise.try and module sources passing: 96,229 of 96,230 executions, one documented expected failure, no corrections.

blocks.text: Upstream test262 at `d53ebc8b` adds 236 executions the engine failed, and `6739da17` implements what they test: `Iterator.prototype.chunks` and `windows` from the stage 4 iterator chunking proposal, `Iterator.prototype.includes`, the 2^53-1 limit on `take` and `drop`, `Promise.try` returning through PromiseResolve, and the test262 host's module-source object. `a57c51b4` fixed iterator closing beside it: it resumed every generator with the intrinsic `return`, so an overridden `return` was never called. `67a7e1cc` moves the security workflow's Test262 job to the new pin and runs the corpus once, unmodified: 96,229 of 96,230 executions pass with zero skips, and the DateTimeFormat ECMA-402 shard 490 of 490. The one expected failure is `annexB/language/function-code/block-decl-func-skip-arguments.js` in sloppy mode, whose final assertion is ES2017 wording that ES2018 deleted (Node fails it too). The other eight expected-failure entries went with upstream's own fixes, and with them the five correction patches and the second, patched run. A debug-assertion run of the corpus found one more defect, a meaningless heap read when `Promise.all` steps a primitive iterable (`1fb485f3`).

Two other checks came back. The engine's tests no longer compiled on arm64 after the superinstruction pass added a field the aarch64 JIT's tests did not set, and two register-file accessors were dead code off x86-64, which `-Dwarnings` turns into an error (`57374b30`). The engine and its tests now build warning-free for aarch64 Linux and macOS, and the engine with the CLI's features for armv7 Linux. And the Python corpus now runs on the CPU path and expects CPython 3.13's rule for a final `**` glob, so all 196 programs match CPython 3.13.14, in the default, no-fast-path, interpreter and no-Python-JIT modes (`57068197`). `bdbdc2b1` recorded a dependency edge the sandbox and WebAssembly lockfiles were missing.

entries.title: Release packaging: one .wasm per engine and plain native files
entries.summary: As 0.0.26 ships it: each WebAssembly engine is one .wasm carrying its own bindings, one loader runs any of them in a default-deny sandbox, and native downloads are plain files, Linux arm64 and armv7 included.

blocks.text: 0.0.26 changes what a release ships. Every WebAssembly engine is a single file, `zipp-<version>-javascript.wasm`, `-javascript-lite.wasm`, `-javascript-python.wasm` or `-javascript-python-base.wasm`, beside `zipp-<version>-torch-package.wasm`. Each engine carries the JavaScript bindings generated for exactly that build in a custom section, with a record of its version, commit and variant, so a glue file can no longer meet another build's module. One loader, `zipp.mjs`, reads that record and those bindings and runs any of the engines in a page, a Worker, Node, Deno or Bun. It ships in `zipp-<version>-wasm-embed-kit.zip` with its types, the host SDK, the GPU lab, the docs and examples.

A sandbox made by that loader starts with no storage, no files, no network and no host functions, and each is granted explicitly: a private in-memory `localStorage`, a map of files to read (and to write, if allowed), a `fetch` that reaches only listed origins or URL prefixes and sends no cookies, and named host functions. An instruction budget stops runaway computation inside the engine, and each sandbox runs in its own Worker by default, which a time limit terminates. Native downloads are plain files: a Windows portable `.exe`, a Windows `.msi` that installs per user and adds `zipp` to the user's PATH, and Linux binaries for x86-64, arm64 and armv7. This site gains a [sandbox playground](/sandbox/playground/) for the new loader, which runs the 0.0.26 JavaScript engine.

entries.title: Plain downloads, one-file engines, and v0.0.26
entries.summary: v0.0.26 ships plain native files and one .wasm per engine with a default-deny sandbox loader, passes the latest Test262 unmodified on 64-bit and 32-bit builds, and imports torch in WebKit in under 0.4 s instead of about 32 s.

blocks.text: [v0.0.26](https://github.com/f2i-com/zipp.org/releases/tag/v0.0.26) was published on 18 October from `5f1c0578`, the first release of plain files. Windows gets `zipp-0.0.26-windows-x86_64-portable.exe` (17,624,064 bytes) and `zipp-0.0.26-windows-x86_64-installer.msi` (5,718,016), which installs per user into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\ZIPP` and adds `zipp` to the user's PATH with no administrator rights. Linux gets `zipp-0.0.26-linux-x86_64`, `-linux-arm64` and `-linux-armv7`, the last for 32-bit Arm with hard float and interpreter only; they need glibc 2.35 or later and `chmod +x`. The WebAssembly engines are four `.wasm` files and the torch package, each engine carrying its own bindings, and `zipp-0.0.26-wasm-embed-kit.zip` holds `zipp.mjs`, which loads any of them and runs programs in a Worker with nothing permitted unless granted. As published, the JavaScript engine is 4,673,483 bytes and 1,197,743 after Brotli; without its bindings, 1,184,942 after Brotli, 3.3% more than v0.0.25's 1,146,621. The [sandbox playground](/sandbox/playground/) runs it.

Test262 at the corpus of 13 October 2026 (`d53ebc8b`), unmodified, passes 96,229 of 96,230 executions with one expected Annex B failure, and so do a 32-bit build, which CI now runs as a Windows i686 job (`65c1c1d8`), and the arm64 Linux CLI built on an Arm runner. Indices and lengths past 2^32 had been truncated on 32-bit hosts, wasm32 and armv7, in every earlier WebAssembly release too, and are exact now (`2d337999`). The first `import torch` in a fresh engine falls from about 32 s to under 0.4 s in WebKit, from 0.64 s to about 0.27 s in Chromium and from 0.78 s to about 0.3 s in Node (`7eb926e9`, `f091e2fe`, `a4099b74`). Over the cycle, on canonical held-out builds, the interpreter went from 1.199× to 0.931× of Bellard's QuickJS's time on the [21 expansion workloads](/journal/twenty-one-new-workloads-against-quickjs/) and from 0.834× to 0.791× on the 17 hostile ones.

entries.title: Seven reports from @takahashim, and v0.0.27
entries.summary: Seven more issues from @takahashim, from a regex that never finished compiling to an abort flag that slowed every instruction, are fixed, and v0.0.27 adds a Brotli copy of every WebAssembly engine.

blocks.text: @takahashim, whose ten reports shaped [v0.0.25](/journal/ten-embedding-bugs-and-v0-0-25/), sent seven more after v0.0.26, each with a minimal repro and most with a pointer to the cause. Nested quantified groups such as `(?:(?:a|)+|)+` made the regex optimizer copy every level below each loop it unrolled: depth 20 took 1.6 s to compile, depth 31 never finished, and from depth 17 a 16-bit loop counter overflowed and panicked the safe-sandbox engine (#58). Unrolling now has a per-regex budget and the compiled-size cap is checked while the program is emitted, so depth 31 compiles in about a millisecond (`54906ffe`). Alternation is built as a shallow tree that keeps its alternatives' order, so the safe-sandbox profile no longer stops at 64 of them and 200,000 compile on a 1 MiB stack (#57, `351a1912`). In a large function a statement outside a loop gives its scratch registers back, so a bundle of more than about 33,000 statements compiles (#56, `9356ecb2`).

An installed abort flag had sent every instruction down the full metering path, about seven times slower; it is now read on its own stride from the countdown, and an abort still lands within 4,096 instructions (#62, `ed40ce85`). Native safe-sandbox builds have `SharedArrayBuffer` and `Atomics` again, backed by agent-local bytes, while the WebAssembly engines keep a guest surface with no shared-memory globals (#61, `ec67592e`, `7682df51`, `05d2bd9b`); the writing Atomics operations revalidate the access after converting their value (#59), and `super()` into `%TypedArray%` throws (#60). Every WebAssembly engine is now also published as a Brotli `.wasm.br`, which the embed kit's loader 1.2.0 reads however it is served (`81329040`). [v0.0.27](https://github.com/f2i-com/zipp.org/releases/tag/v0.0.27) was published on 18 October from `74d92e70`.

entries.title: Eleven reports from @takahashim, a faster interpreter, and v0.0.28
entries.summary: Eleven more issues from @takahashim, among them `import.meta.url`, unhandled-rejection reports and V8-format stacks, are fixed, and v0.0.28's interpreter runs Babel and the TypeScript compiler more than twice as fast as v0.0.27.

blocks.text: @takahashim, whose seven reports shaped [v0.0.27](/journal/seven-embedding-fixes-and-v0-0-27/), sent eleven more, the last four as proposals with a working design. A regex that reached its step ceiling could not be caught once a host set limits; it is now a `RangeError` the script can catch, and a host can set the ceiling and the hardened profile's other caps per VM (#69, `6f730a8d`, `ff104592`). A full heap is reported as the heap's rather than a regex's (#70, `4b94c120`), `new` on a Proxy of an arrow throws before its trap (#71, `1c43deca`), a scope indexes its names once it holds 16, so 6,400 `var`s compile in 8 ms instead of 352 (#72, `c0d9527b`), re-arming the heap ceiling collects only after a budget found the heap at it (#73, `72eda1aa`), `resource_usage()` reads an O(1) estimate (#74, `cf8439d1`), and a top-level `const` destructuring binds under script semantics (#75, `dcbe4695`).

Modules have `import.meta.url` (#76, `68f9e393`); unhandled rejections are reported to the host, and `zipp` ends with status 1 on one, as Node does (#77, `bcd4174d`); `Error.prototype.stack` gives V8-format frames placed where V8 places them (#78, `fced020a`); and `ScriptState::run_script` runs a classic script (#79, `0509416c`). Over the same weeks the interpreter got faster on large programs: Babel's workload takes 5.2 s instead of 11.3 s, a program of 256 or more functions runs with its JIT off (`ca511f54`), and a `switch` over string literals is one table lookup (`b63fc659`). [v0.0.28](https://github.com/f2i-com/zipp.org/releases/tag/v0.0.28) was published on 21 October from `da0fe6b1`.
